question: How does loss of plasticity develop across attention and feed-forward components of Vision Transformers in task-incremental learning, and can recent-gradient geometry be used to preserve adaptation to newly encountered tasks?

key_findings.claim: The diagnostic study reports substantial plasticity loss in ViT-B/16 despite greater resilience than a capacity-matched MLP.
key_findings.evidence: Across the long diagnostic stream, vanilla ViT reaches AAT 0.590, described as a 14.9% degradation relative to a model and optimizer reinitialized at every task. A one-block ViT and full ViT outperform the MLP, while freezing the first 11 of 12 ViT blocks improves over fully updating the model, suggesting that retaining stable early representations can outweigh end-to-end adaptation.

key_findings.claim: The paper's stated diagnostic protocol is internally inconsistent: CIFAR-100 cannot form 200 disjoint five-class tasks, and the appendix even labels a sampled task 201.
key_findings.evidence: Section 4.1 says CIFAR-100 forms a sequence of 200 tasks with five classes per task, which would require 1,000 class assignments if tasks were disjoint, while CIFAR-100 has 100 classes. Figure 3 runs to task 200 and Appendix Figure 26 samples tasks 1, 51, 101, 151, and 201. Section 6 separately and coherently defines disjoint CIFAR-100 streams of 10, 20, and 25 tasks. No repetition, reshuffling, or resampling rule reconciles the 200-task diagnostic stream.

key_findings.claim: Plasticity degradation is depth-amplified and module-dependent: FFNs show the strongest collapse, while attention becomes unstable mainly in deeper blocks and its value projections deteriorate more than query or key projections.
key_findings.evidence: Feature effective rank remains comparatively stable in shallow blocks but contracts in deeper blocks; weight magnitudes grow faster with depth. FFN layers have lower effective rank, stronger magnitude growth, and an increasing fraction of dead units. Across attention heads, V matrices have less stable effective rank than Q and K. The CLS-token trajectory mirrors these effects, preserving rank early and contracting through FFNs and deep attention.

key_findings.claim: Localized reset and activation interventions do not restore ViT plasticity in the reported setting, while update-regulating TRAC is consistently stronger.
key_findings.evidence: Five CBP replacement schedules give only marginal improvements; NaP and CReLU give negligible or negative gains, whereas TRAC preserves higher rank and suppresses weight growth. On the first 25 diagnostic tasks, CReLU has AAT 0.617 versus vanilla ViT 0.638 and the reset upper bound 0.732, while the appendix states that CReLU doubles cost.

key_findings.claim: ARROW adds direction-aware preconditioning to step-size regulation by inverting a damped, rank-W covariance of recent gradients.
key_findings.evidence: At step t, the update is -eta_t(alpha_t I + beta C_t)^-1 g_t with C_t equal to the average of g_i g_i^T over a W-step window. Eigen-directions repeatedly represented in recent gradients are attenuated by 1/(alpha + beta lambda), while neglected directions are relatively amplified. The Woodbury identity reduces inversion to a W-by-W system using a d-by-W gradient buffer, with SGD- or RMS-like warm-up until the window fills.

key_findings.claim: The ablation supports curvature strength and damping as active ingredients and finds that applying ARROW only to the last attention block works better than applying it broadly.
key_findings.evidence: On CIFAR-100 with 10 tasks, last-block ARROW obtains 64.21% AAT. Applying it to all blocks gives 63.96% and to the last six gives 63.94%. Setting beta=0 yields 59.85%, and setting alpha=1 with beta=0.9 yields 59.31%. The location result agrees with the paper's deep-attention diagnosis, but the method does not directly repair the FFN module identified as the larger bottleneck.

key_findings.claim: ARROW has the highest reported AAT in all six CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-R streams, but its margin over the strongest baseline ranges from large to very small.
key_findings.evidence: For CIFAR-100 with 10, 20, and 25 tasks, ARROW scores 64.21, 73.52, and 73.89 versus TRAC 63.58, 73.32, and 72.19 and vanilla 57.21, 66.53, and 70.93. For ImageNet-R with 20, 40, and 50 tasks, ARROW scores 37.20, 37.59, and 43.40; the strongest non-ARROW scores are 30.83 (L2P), 37.35 (NaP), and 42.06 (NaP), while vanilla scores 28.16, 36.94, and 40.61. The advantage is 0.20 points over TRAC on CIFAR-20 and 0.24 over NaP on ImageNet-R-40, but 6.37 over L2P on ImageNet-R-20.

key_findings.claim: ARROW is tuning-sensitive and simple decay schedules do not improve its best fixed setting.
key_findings.evidence: The coarse search spans alpha from 1 to 1e-5, beta from 0.3 to 1.3, W from 10 to 30, and two warm-ups. With W=20 and RMS-like warm-up, alpha=1e-3 and beta=0.9 gives 63.96%, while alpha=5e-2 gives 61.46%. Global and per-task exponential alpha decays at 0.999, 0.99, 0.98, and 0.97 do not beat the selected fixed configuration.

key_findings.claim: The manuscript does not fully answer its own computational-cost question, and the headline ARROW configuration's dependence on TRAC step-size adaptation is ambiguous.
key_findings.evidence: Q4 asks for time and memory overhead, but the result section only says W=20 is 'comparable' to vanilla ViT and gives no numeric throughput, memory, or complexity measurement. Appendix C defines a 'trac' suffix as introducing TRAC's adaptive learning rate; the best 0.6396 tuning configuration carries that suffix, while the main tables omit a column stating whether headline ARROW includes TRAC. Therefore the incremental effect of covariance reshaping versus its step-size controller is not cleanly documented.

key_findings.claim: The gradient covariance is a useful empirical second-moment preconditioner, but calling it an online curvature estimate requires assumptions that the paper does not test.
key_findings.evidence: C_t is defined only as an uncentered recent-gradient outer-product average. It equals an empirical-Fisher-like curvature proxy under model and sampling assumptions, not the Hessian in general. No comparison against measured Hessian/Fisher eigenvectors, K-FAC/Kron, or a centered covariance is reported, so the claimed geometry mechanism is plausible but not directly validated.

method.core_idea: Diagnose plasticity loss at the level of ViT depth, attention projections, FFNs, CLS-token representations, and neuron activity, then preserve new-task adaptability by preconditioning recent gradients with a damped low-rank online second-moment matrix, principally in the deepest attention block.
method.mechanism: ARROW buffers the last W gradients for a targeted parameter block, forms C_t=(1/W) sum g_i g_i^T, and applies the inverse of alpha I + beta C_t to the current gradient. Frequently used recent directions receive smaller updates and low-eigenvalue directions receive relatively larger updates, broadening the effective update subspace under distribution shift. Woodbury computes the action of the inverse through the d-by-W gradient matrix and a W-by-W solve rather than materializing a d-by-d matrix. RMS-like or SGD warm-up is used before the buffer fills; the selected setup uses W=20, alpha around 1e-3, beta=0.9, and targets the last attention block.
assumptions: Task identity is available to the task-incremental learner, so task-inference error is excluded from the plasticity analysis.
AAT on newly encountered class partitions primarily measures plasticity rather than base model quality, task difficulty, retention, or classifier-head design.
Recent uncentered gradient outer products are aligned closely enough with relevant Hessian or Fisher curvature to guide directional preconditioning.
A W=20 window is long enough to estimate dominant directions and short enough to track abrupt distribution shifts.
The extra d-by-W gradient-state memory and W-by-W solve are practical for the selected attention parameter group.
The best last-block intervention generalizes beyond the particular ViT-B/16, task order, data preprocessing, and hyperparameter search used here.
Effective rank, stable rank, weight norm, and active-unit fraction are meaningful proxies for plasticity rather than merely correlates of architecture and optimization scale.
Baseline methods receive sufficiently comparable tuning and compute budgets to attribute Table 3 differences to mitigation quality.
The unexplained 200-task diagnostic stream is generated by a valid non-stationary protocol despite the impossible literal description of disjoint five-class CIFAR-100 tasks.

techniques.role: Tracks effective/stable feature rank, weight rank and magnitude, CLS-token rank, and FFN active/dead units across blocks and tasks.
Separates Q, K, and V behavior across individual heads to identify value projections as the least stable attention component.
Reinitializes model and optimizer at each task to approximate unencumbered current-task learnability.
Uses an online W-sample gradient outer-product matrix as a low-rank geometry proxy.
Computes the damped inverse-covariance action through a W-dimensional system instead of a full parameter-space inverse.
Provides stable first-order updates until enough gradients exist to populate the covariance window.
Applies geometry-aware updates only to the last attention block, which empirically outperforms all-block and last-six-block variants.

limitations: Author-stated: ARROW introduces multiple damping, curvature, window, and warm-up hyperparameters and is sensitive to their tuning.
Author-stated: AAT is not fully objective when methods have different base-performance levels.

Reviewer-identified: the 200-task CIFAR-100 diagnostic description is arithmetically impossible as written and is inconsistent with the explicit disjoint 10/20/25-task protocol; this prevents reproduction of the central layerwise diagnosis.

Reviewer-identified: crucial training details are absent, including task order construction, image resizing/augmentation for ViT-B/16 on 32x32 CIFAR inputs, epochs or updates per task, base optimizer and learning rates, classifier-head handling, number of random seeds, and baseline tuning budgets.
Reviewer-identified: Table 3 reports no uncertainty or significance; several wins are only 0.20-0.65 percentage points, so they may be within seed variance.

Reviewer-identified: AAT across streams with different classes per task is not a controlled function of stream length—the longer CIFAR streams have fewer classes per classification problem—so rising AAT cannot demonstrate improved long-horizon robustness.
Reviewer-identified: only current/new-task accuracy is reported; retention, backward transfer, forgetting, calibration, and class-incremental inference without task IDs are not measured.
Reviewer-identified: C_t is an uncentered gradient second moment, not generally a Hessian; no curvature-alignment or eigenvector validation supports the claimed second-order interpretation.

Reviewer-identified: ARROW targets the last attention block even though the diagnosis calls FFN collapse the structural bottleneck; the causal path from diagnosis to chosen intervention is therefore incomplete.
Reviewer-identified: the paper asks about time and memory overhead but provides no numeric wall-time, throughput, peak-memory, state-size, or scaling results.

Reviewer-identified: Appendix C indicates that tuned configurations may add TRAC adaptive learning rates, but the headline tables do not make that dependency explicit; a matched ARROW-without-TRAC comparison is missing.

Reviewer-identified: evaluation covers one ViT family, two image-classification datasets, and at most 50 coherently defined disjoint tasks; no pre-trained foundation ViT, larger-resolution model, language transformer, streaming task-free setting, or indefinite sequence is tested.

Reviewer-identified: the paper provides equations but no pseudocode or released implementation link, leaving parameter grouping, covariance buffering, numerical solves, and optimizer-state interactions underspecified.
failure_modes: Large alpha suppresses the directional effect, while overly small damping can make the low-rank solve poorly conditioned; alpha is empirically the most sensitive hyperparameter.
A short window produces a noisy geometry estimate, whereas a long window mixes obsolete tasks and increases state and solve cost; W=10 and W=30 generally trail W=20 in the reported search.
Applying ARROW to every block slightly underperforms targeting only the last block, so indiscriminate geometry correction can dilute or disrupt useful shallow representations.
Removing beta or weakening the inverse rescaling drops AAT toward first-order performance, showing that a nominal ARROW wrapper is insufficient without tuned curvature strength.
CBP-style local unit replacement cannot restore coupled attention-FFN geometry and provides only marginal gains in these ViTs.
CReLU lowers AAT from 0.638 to 0.617 over the first 25 diagnostic tasks while doubling stated cost.
For ImageNet-R-40, ARROW improves only 0.24 points over NaP; for CIFAR-20, only 0.20 over TRAC, leaving small-margin regimes vulnerable to seed noise.
An abrupt task shift can make the pre-shift gradient buffer actively misaligned with the new objective until the W-step window refreshes.
Because main ARROW appears to inherit a TRAC-style adaptive step size, an incorrectly initialized or warm-started controller can confound the intended directional correction.
Task-incremental AAT can look better simply because each later benchmark stream has fewer classes per task, masking failure to retain old tasks or infer task identity.
reusable_insights: Diagnose heterogeneous models per depth and component; a single network-level plasticity metric can hide stable shallow attention, unstable deep attention, and more severe FFN collapse.
Separate update magnitude from update direction: scalar learning-rate control and curvature-aware preconditioning address different sources of adaptation failure.
A short rolling gradient subspace is a practical route to online preconditioning when full curvature is impossible, but it should be validated against task-shift timescales.
Targeted intervention can outperform applying the same optimizer everywhere; use diagnostics to choose parameter groups and retain stable early features.
Track both representation rank and neuron utilization: spectral contraction and dormant units expose distinct capacity bottlenecks.
Report a from-scratch-per-task reference when measuring plasticity, but do not call it an upper bound without specifying identical data, compute, and classifier handling.
Compare stream lengths only after controlling per-task label-space difficulty; otherwise AAT changes mix plasticity with easier classification.
When building on an adaptive optimizer, ablate the inherited scalar controller so the contribution of a new directional transform is identifiable.
open_questions: What is the exact reproducible construction of the claimed 200-task CIFAR-100 diagnostic stream?
Does ARROW still win with matched seed counts, confidence intervals, and equal hyperparameter-search budgets for TRAC, Kron/K-FAC, NaP, and L2P?
How much of the headline gain comes from TRAC-style eta_t adaptation versus the inverse recent-gradient covariance?
Do the eigenvectors of C_t align with measured Hessian, generalized Gauss-Newton, or empirical-Fisher directions at task boundaries?
Would targeting FFN layers, or jointly preconditioning the last attention and FFN modules, better address the paper's own diagnosis?
Can a sketched, diagonal-plus-low-rank, or Kronecker implementation reduce the d-by-W memory and W-by-W solve cost without losing gains?
How should W adapt to task duration and abruptness instead of remaining fixed at 20 steps?
Does ARROW preserve both new-task plasticity and old-task retention in class-incremental or task-free evaluation without task IDs?
Do benefits persist for pretrained large ViTs, higher-resolution datasets, multimodal transformers, and streams much longer than 50 well-defined tasks?
Why do deep attention blocks benefit most from ARROW when the largest measured rank and dead-unit degradation occurs in FFNs?

competitive_landscape.title: Loss of plasticity in deep continual learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: foundational direct predecessor and source of the continual-backpropagation baseline
competitive_landscape.difference: Dohare et al. establish long-run plasticity loss across ImageNet and reinforcement learning and argue that continual random unit replacement preserves diversity indefinitely. The reviewed paper tests that intervention in ViT FFNs, finds it weak in the coupled attention-FFN architecture, and instead uses targeted update preconditioning; however, its much shorter and underspecified streams do not establish indefinite preservation.

competitive_landscape.title: Fast TRAC: A Parameter-Free Optimizer for Lifelong Reinforcement Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: closest update-regulation baseline and apparent scalar-step component of ARROW
competitive_landscape.difference: TRAC uses parameter-free online-convex-optimization machinery to adapt regularization or step scale without curvature and is evaluated in lifelong RL. ARROW adds a tuned low-rank directional preconditioner for supervised ViT task streams; Appendix naming suggests it may retain TRAC's adaptive eta, so the new contribution is the directional transform rather than a wholly independent optimizer stack.
competitive_landscape.source_version: NeurIPS 2024 poster OpenReview revision, last modified 2024-11-06

competitive_landscape.title: Spectral Collapse Drives Loss of Plasticity in Deep Continual Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: omitted direct predecessor linking plasticity, feature rank, Hessian spectrum, and curvature-aware remedies
competitive_landscape.difference: Prakash et al. show that Hessian spectral collapse precedes plasticity loss, formalize trainability rank conditions, and motivate effective-feature-rank plus L2 regularization through Kronecker-factored curvature. The reviewed paper adds ViT component-level Q/K/V, FFN, and CLS diagnostics and replaces regularization with a recent-gradient covariance inverse, but the broad rank-and-curvature explanation is prior rather than novel.

competitive_landscape.title: Continual Learning with Query-Only Attention
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct prior on attention architecture, ViT plasticity, and curvature-rank behavior
competitive_landscape.difference: Bekal et al. simplify full attention to query-only attention, report improved plasticity and forgetting versus selective reinitialization, and connect retained plasticity to higher Hessian rank. The reviewed paper keeps standard ViT attention, provides more granular depth/module diagnostics, and intervenes through optimization rather than architecture.

competitive_landscape.title: Stable Gradients for Stable Learning at Scale in Deep Reinforcement Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct curvature-aware optimizer and depth-dependent non-stationarity predecessor cited as Kron
competitive_landscape.difference: Castanyer et al. diagnose dormant units, rank loss, vanishing curvature, and depth-amplified gradient failure, then use Kronecker-factored Fisher preconditioning (Kron) and multi-skip residuals in non-stationary supervised learning and deep RL. ARROW uses a simpler sliding low-rank empirical gradient covariance and targets the last ViT attention block, but does not compare directly with Kron despite closely overlapping directional-preconditioning motivation.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim a systematic first fine-grained account of plasticity loss in heterogeneous ViTs and a novel geometry-aware optimizer, ARROW, that preserves effective update rank through an online low-rank curvature estimate.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper tracks feature and parameter ranks, norms, CLS-token dynamics, Q/K/V projections, and dead FFN units across depth; tests reset, normalization, activation, prompt, and optimizer baselines; derives a windowed covariance preconditioner; and reports the best AAT in six CIFAR-100/ImageNet-R task streams with term and location ablations.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The narrow novelty is the combination of component-level ViT diagnosis with a Woodbury-computed recent-gradient outer-product preconditioner targeted at deep attention. The broader claims are not new: prior primary work already establishes ViT-specific plasticity and Hessian-rank effects, feature/Hessian spectral collapse, depth-dependent gradient pathologies, Kronecker curvature preconditioning, and adaptive step regulation. The paper omits the especially direct Spectral Collapse predecessor and does not cleanly distinguish ARROW's covariance transform from its apparent TRAC step-size component. Novelty and confidence are further narrowed by the irreconcilable 200-task protocol and missing reproducibility and compute details.

reviewer_notes: Read all 26 extracted pages end to end: main text and complete references on pages 1-13, diagnostic appendices A.1-A.5 on pages 14-24, CReLU negative result on page 24, and full hyperparameter appendices on pages 25-26. The extraction has usable text on 26/26 pages. Multi-panel figures and the 200/201 task labels were additionally checked with Ghostscript's layout-preserving PDF renderer; no PDF text resolves the protocol contradiction. Competitor discovery used at least three protocol query families: (1) ViT/attention plasticity with effective rank, dormant FFNs, and Hessian collapse; (2) CIFAR task-incremental AAT with CBP, NaP, TRAC, L2P, and deep-block baselines; and (3) the paper's 'geometry-aware', low-rank online covariance, second-order, and direction-reshaping novelty language plus cited Kron and TRAC predecessors. Official arXiv, OpenReview, NeurIPS, and Nature records were checked on 2026-08-23. Prior work already contains rank/curvature diagnosis and direction-aware optimization, but not the exact recent-gradient-window preconditioner applied to the last ViT attention block. This is a primary full-text pass, not a second-reviewer verification.
